interactions.label: Why are radionuclide bone scans often falsely negative in multiple myeloma?

params.question: Why are radionuclide bone scans often falsely negative in multiple myeloma?

answers.text: Myeloma lesions are too small to be detected by gamma cameras

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Size is not the issue. The lesions can be quite large. The problem is that bone scans rely on osteoblast activity for tracer uptake, which is suppressed in myeloma.

answers.text: Myeloma cells secrete DKK1, which inhibits osteoblast activity needed for tracer uptake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DKK1 blocks osteoblast Wnt signalling, so no new bone forms around the lesion. Since bone scans detect osteoblastic activity, not bone destruction, they miss purely lytic myeloma lesions. Plain X-ray or MRI is preferred.

answers.text: Bone scan tracers cannot penetrate the axial skeleton where myeloma lesions predominate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone scan tracers reach the axial skeleton normally. The issue is that tracer uptake depends on osteoblast activity, which is specifically suppressed in myeloma by DKK1.

answers.text: Myeloma produces sclerotic lesions that do not absorb the radiotracer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic, not sclerotic. Sclerotic lesions would actually show increased uptake on bone scan. The false negativity arises because DKK1 shuts down osteoblast activity entirely.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the DKK1 pathway: myeloma cells secrete DKK1, which blocks osteoblast Wnt signalling. No osteoblast activity means no tracer uptake on bone scan, making it unreliable for detecting myeloma lesions.
Well done. DKK1 inhibition of osteoblasts is the mechanism behind the falsely negative bone scan — a favourite exam point in myeloma diagnosis.

params.question: In the bone marrow microenvironment, interleukin-6 produced by stromal cells and myeloma cells primarily serves to:

answers.text: Activate osteoclasts and promote lytic bone destruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osteoclast activation in myeloma is driven by RANK ligand (RANKL), not interleukin-6. IL-6 has a different role in sustaining the malignant clone itself.

answers.text: Drive clonal expansion of myeloma cells and block their apoptosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IL-6 is the principal survival factor for the myeloma clone. Both stromal cells and the myeloma cells themselves produce it, creating a self-sustaining loop that drives proliferation and prevents programmed cell death.

answers.text: Stimulate erythropoiesis to compensate for marrow replacement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IL-6 does not stimulate erythropoiesis. In fact, myeloma-associated IL-6 contributes to the inflammatory milieu that suppresses red cell production, worsening the anaemia.

answers.text: Enhance glomerular filtration of free light chains

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IL-6 has no role in renal filtration. Free light chains cross the glomerulus because of their small size, not because of any cytokine effect. Renal damage results from cast formation, not enhanced filtration.

overallFeedback.feedback: IL-6 is the principal growth and survival factor for myeloma cells. Stromal cells and the myeloma cells themselves both produce it, forming a self-sustaining loop. Do not confuse it with RANKL, which drives osteoclast-mediated bone destruction.
Exactly right. The IL-6 autocrine–paracrine loop is central to myeloma biology — it sustains the malignant clone and is a therapeutic target.

interactions.label: A patient with suspected multiple myeloma has a negative urine dipstick for prot

params.question: A patient with suspected multiple myeloma has a negative urine dipstick for protein. Which of the following best explains this finding?

answers.text: The patient has no proteinuria and myeloma can be excluded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A negative dipstick does NOT exclude myeloma-related proteinuria. The dipstick detects albumin, not free light chains (Bence-Jones protein), so it can be falsely reassuring.

answers.text: Monoclonal light chains are too large to pass through the glomerular filtration barrier

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Free light chains (kappa and lambda) are small enough to cross the glomerulus freely. That is precisely why they appear in urine as Bence-Jones protein.

answers.text: The standard urine dipstick detects albumin but not free light chains (Bence-Jones protein)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The urine dipstick is designed to detect albumin. Free light chains are not picked up, making the dipstick falsely negative in myeloma. Always order urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) or urine immunofixation when myeloma is suspected.

answers.text: Bence-Jones protein is found only in serum and is never excreted in urine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bence-Jones protein is specifically defined as free light chains in the urine. They readily cross the glomerulus and are a hallmark urine finding in myeloma. The issue is that the dipstick method cannot detect them.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the standard urine dipstick detects albumin, not Bence-Jones protein (free light chains). A negative dipstick is falsely reassuring in myeloma. Order urine protein electrophoresis or immunofixation instead.
Correct. This is a classic diagnostic pitfall — always request UPEP or urine immunofixation when myeloma is on the differential, regardless of dipstick results.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old woman has an M-protein on serum protein electrophoresis. Bone marr

params.question: A 58-year-old woman has an M-protein on serum protein electrophoresis. Bone marrow biopsy shows 6 percent clonal plasma cells. She has no anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, or bone lesions. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Active myeloma requires at least 10 percent clonal plasma cells in the marrow AND a myeloma-defining event (CRAB or biomarker criteria). This patient meets neither threshold.

Smouldering myeloma requires 10 percent or more marrow plasma cells and/or an M-protein of 30 g/L or more, without CRAB features. With only 6 percent plasma cells, the threshold for smouldering myeloma is not met.

Correct. MGUS is defined by an M-protein with marrow plasma cells below 10 percent and no CRAB features. The annual progression risk to myeloma is approximately 1 percent, so these patients require long-term monitoring, not treatment.

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma that specifically secretes IgM and presents with hyperviscosity syndrome. Without knowing the immunoglobulin class is IgM or seeing hyperviscosity features, this diagnosis cannot be made.

overallFeedback.feedback: Apply the IMWG framework: M-protein present + marrow plasma cells below 10 percent + no CRAB features = MGUS. Above 10 percent without CRAB = smouldering myeloma. Above 10 percent with any CRAB feature or biomarker criterion = active myeloma.

Well analysed. Distinguishing MGUS from smouldering and active myeloma requires careful application of the IMWG thresholds — marrow plasma cell percentage and presence of myeloma-defining events are the key discriminators.
